Q: What are best practices for logging and monitoring in production backend systems? A:

1. Structure: Logging as Data

Avoid plain text. Modern logs should be structured (JSON) . This allows log aggregators to index fields, enabling you to run queries like GET /api/v1/orders WHERE user_id = '123' AND response_time > 500ms.

  • Correlation IDs: Every request must have a unique request_id generated at the gateway or entry point. Pass this ID through every internal function, service call, and database query.

  • Standard Metadata: Every log entry should automatically include:

    • timestamp (ISO 8601 UTC).

    • service_name and version.

    • level (INFO, WARN, ERROR).

    • correlation_id.

    • environment (prod, staging).

2. What to Log (The "Golden Trio")

Logging too much is expensive and noisy; logging too little is useless. Aim for these three layers:

  1. Request/Response Context: Log high-level metadata (HTTP method, URL, status code, latency). Never log PII (passwords, credit cards, emails) or raw binary payloads.

  2. State Transitions: Log key business events, not every line of code. (e.g., "OrderCreated", "PaymentProcessed").

  3. Error Context: When an error occurs, include the stack trace , the inputs that caused the error, and the user context.

3. Integration: Logs vs. Metrics vs. Tracing

Logs tell you what happened; Metrics tell you how much , and Traces tell you where .

  • Metrics: Use these for system health. Track request rates, error rates, and duration (latency). If your error rate spikes, the metric alerts you; you then jump to the logs for the specific correlation_id to see the error.

  • Distributed Tracing: If you move to microservices, you need a tracing system. It allows you to visualize the lifecycle of a request as it hops between services, showing exactly which service caused the delay or failure.

4. Common Pitfalls

  • Logging PII (Personally Identifiable Information): Compliance issues (GDPR/SOC2) will arise if you log sensitive data. Implement a sanitization layer or "scrubber" before logs hit the disk.

  • Blocking I/O: Never perform synchronous file writing inside your application loop. Use an asynchronous appender or ship logs via a sidecar/agent process to avoid slowing down your API.

  • Log Level Inflation: Avoid logging DEBUG or VERBOSE messages in production. If you need them, implement Dynamic Log Levels so you can flip them to DEBUG via an admin toggle without restarting the service.

  • The "Log Dump" Anti-pattern: Don't dump entire objects or database results. Log only the fields relevant to identifying the failure.

If you want to achieve professional-grade observability, look into the OpenTelemetry (OTel) standard. It is vendor-neutral and designed to handle logging, metrics, and tracing in a unified way, preventing you from being locked into a specific monitoring tool later on.

Q: arr.reduce method return accumulator the first argument A:

arr.reduce method return the accumulator which is the first argument. So why the last value of array is return in my code.

See the documentation on MDN:

The reduce() method is an iterative method. It runs a "reducer" callback function over all elements in the array, in ascending-index order, and accumulates them into a single value. Every time, the return value of callbackFn is passed into callbackFn again on next invocation as accumulator. The final value of accumulator (which is the value returned from callbackFn on the final iteration of the array) becomes the return value of reduce().

The accumulator is passed in to the callback function as the first argument, but it is determined by the return value of the callback function.

The result of evaluating the expression obj[value.id] = value is value so in the second example you are returning value from the callback function instead of obj from the function.

Q: MySQL ERROR 2013 (HY000): Lost connection to MySQL server during query A:

Problem solved, although without knowing exactly what caused it. I uninstalled the MySQL server completely, deleted all the tables, reinstalled the server, re-initialised it, and restored the database dump. This time, the restore was successful. I assume, as @LSemi suggested, that there was corruption in the InnoDB tablespace.

Q: Pass TextBox Data to RDLC report A:

You have to set parameter value and pass it to your report:

Dim parReportParam1 As New ReportParameter("parReportParam1", Me.TextBox1.Text)
Me.YourReportViewer.LocalReport.SetParameters(New ReportParameter() {parReportParam1})

In your report you must set textbox value as:

=Parameters!parReportParam1.Value
